author: Epiphanius of Salamis
addressee: Christians who make and venerate images of Christ, the Theotokos, martyrs, angels, and prophets
occasion: Epiphanius writes to oppose the practice of making painted images of Christ, Mary, martyrs, angels, and prophets for memorial and honor, which he regards as a return to idolatry.
argument: Epiphanius argues that making images of the saints dishonors rather than honors them, since Scripture promises they will be transformed into glory like Christ and the angels, not depicted in dead, voiceless matter. He shows from Scripture that angels refused worship, directing it to God alone, and he asserts that the apostles likewise did not wish to be worshipped, illustrating this with the example of the apostle who refused worship from Cornelius. He cites the Council of Laodicea's anathema against angel worship. He further argues that the incarnate Christ remains incomprehensible and uncircumscribable, so no one can depict him; the command to make such images comes from the evil one, not from God, who in both Old and New Testaments commands worship of himself alone.

outline.move: Epiphanius opens by condemning those who paint images of Christ, the Theotokos, martyrs, angels, and prophets on plastered walls, and states that such images dishonor rather than honor the saints.
He argues from John and Paul that the saints will be made like Christ in glory, so depicting them in dead, voiceless matter is wrong, and he notes that angels and apostles refused worship.
He cites the refusal of worship by the apostle to Cornelius and the Council of Laodicea's anathema against those who abandon the church to invoke angels, equating this with idolatry.
He argues that the incarnate Christ remains incomprehensible and cannot be depicted, that the command to make such images comes from the evil one, and that God commands worship of himself alone.

scripture: Epiphanius cites the Old Testament in Greek, following Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. Quotations from the prophets and the Law should be cited by their Septuagint names in modern form (e.g., 'the prophet' referring to Psalm 103 LXX = Psalm 104 in Hebrew numbering). New Testament citations follow standard book names. The quotation 'κύριον τὸν θεὸν προσκυνήσεις καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις' is from Deuteronomy 6:13 (cited by Jesus in Matthew 4:10 and Luke 4:8). The angel's words 'Ὅρα μή· σύνδουλος γάρ σου εἰμί...' are from Revelation 19:10 or 22:9. The saying 'ἔσονται ὡς ἄγγελοι θεοῦ' echoes Matthew 22:30 or Mark 12:25. The phrase 'ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα...' is Psalm 103:4 LXX (104:4 Hebrew).
uncertain: The exact date of composition within Epiphanius's lifetime is not established from the text.
The precise identity of the opponents Epiphanius addresses is not named in the surviving text.
Whether the work originally contained more sections beyond the surviving fragments is unknown.
The exact wording of the Council of Laodicea canon quoted is uncertain, as the text gives a paraphrase or adaptation rather than a verbatim citation.
The identity of the unnamed apostle who refused worship from Cornelius is not stated in the text; it is traditionally understood as Peter.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Unnamed apostle (traditionally Peter), source_forms: ["ὁ ἐξουσίαν παρ' αὐτοῦ λαβὼν δεσμεύειν καὶ λύειν ἐπὶ γῆς καὶ οὐρανοῦ"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ γὰρ ἐξουσίαν παρ' αὐτοῦ λαβὼν δεσμεύειν καὶ λύειν ἐπὶ γῆς καὶ οὐρανοῦ, ελεγε Κορνηλίῳ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text does not name the apostle who spoke to Cornelius. The periphrasis "ὁ ἐξουσίαν παρ' αὐτοῦ λαβὼν δεσμεύειν καὶ λύειν ἐπὶ γῆς καὶ οὐρανοῦ" describes someone who received authority to bind and loose on earth and in heaven. In Matthew 16:19 this authority is given to Peter. However, the Cornelius episode in Acts 10 involves Peter (Acts 10:25-26). The brief should note: "Unnamed apostle (Peter, by traditional identification)", with source_forms including "ὁ...ἐξουσίαν...λαβὼν" and the direct speech marker, but the identification as Peter is traditional, not explicit in this text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: An angel (quoted), how_marked: "Quotation marks; speaker identified implicitly through the content and addressee (the seer of Revelation), not by an introductory formula naming the angel"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: «Ορα μή· σύνδουλος γάρ σου εἰμὶ καὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου τῶν ἐχόντων τὴν μαρτυρίαν Ιησοῦ. τῷ θεῷ, φησίν, προσκύνησον»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The angel's words are introduced with quotation marks but no explicit speaker identification in the Greek. However, the content matches Revelation 19:10 and 22:9 where an angel speaks to John the seer. The brief's description is accurate but could be clearer: the speaker is identifiable to readers familiar with Revelation, not purely "implicit"—the quotation's content directly identifies the speaker as an angel through "σύνδουλός σού εἰμι" and the command to worship God. Better: "Speaker identifiable from quotation content as an angel (cf. Revelation 19:10/22:9), with no introductory formula in this text."

_unresolved_facts.claim: Unnamed apostle, traditionally Peter (quoted), how_marked: "Introduced periphrastically as the one who received authority to bind and loose, with ἔλεγε Κορνηλίῳ and quotation marks"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ γὰρ ἐξουσίαν παρ' αὐτοῦ λαβὼν δεσμεύειν καὶ λύειν ἐπὶ γῆς καὶ οὐρανοῦ, ελεγε Κορνηλίῳ ο τι «ὁμοιοπαθής εἰμι κατὰ σὲ ανθρωπος»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The quotation attributed to this figure is only «ὁμοιοπαθής εἰμι κατὰ σὲ ἄνθρωπος» ("I am a man with the same nature as you"). The brief's description suggests the periphrastic introduction includes ἔλεγε Κορνηλίῳ with quotation marks, but the actual structure is: participial phrase describing the figure + ἔλεγε Κορνηλίῳ + ὅτι + quotation. The quotation itself is brief. The brief should clarify that the direct quotation is only "ὁμοιοπαθής εἰμι κατὰ σὲ ἄνθρωπος" and that "ἐδίδασκε μὴ ἑαυτὸν προσκυνεῖσθαι ἀλλὰ τὸν σωτῆρα Χριστόν" is narrative summary, not direct quotation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He shows from Scripture that angels refused worship, directing it to God alone
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: 8 λέγω δὲ ο τι οὐδὲ αὐτοὶ θέλουσι προσκυνεῖσθαι.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Epiphanius states his own conclusion ("λέγω δέ, ὅτι οὐδὲ αὐτοὶ θέλουσι προσκυνεῖσθαι") that angels do not wish to be worshipped, but this is his assertion, not demonstrated "from Scripture" in the immediate context. The scriptural quotation that follows (v.9) is from an angel's speech in Revelation, but the angel there refuses worship for himself as a fellow servant. The brief should say: "He quotes an angel from Revelation who refused worship, and asserts that angels do not wish to be worshipped."

_unresolved_facts.claim: He cites the Council of Laodicea's anathema against those who abandon the church to invoke angels, equating this with idolatry
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: «ει τις ἐγκαταλείπει τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἀγγέλους ὀνομάζει, ἀνάθεμα εστω· οτι ἐγκατέλιπε τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν ̓Ιησοῦν Χριστὸν καὶ εἰδωλολατρείᾳ προσελήλυθε»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Laodicean canon speaks of those who "ἀγγέλους ὀνομάζει" (name/invoke angels), not specifically "abandon the church to invoke angels." The brief's paraphrase "abandon the church to invoke angels" conflates two clauses: ἐγκαταλείπει τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ θεοῦ (abandons the church of God) and ἀγγέλους ὀνομάζει (names/invokes angels). Better: "He cites the Council of Laodicea's anathema against those who abandon the church of God and invoke angels, equating this with abandoning Christ and approaching idolatry."

_unresolved_facts.claim: the apostle who refused worship from Cornelius, declaring himself a fellow human
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ελεγε Κορνηλίῳ ο τι «ὁμοιοπαθής εἰμι κατὰ σὲ ανθρωπος»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Greek says ὁμοιοπαθής εἰμι κατὰ σὲ ἄνθρωπος ("I am a man of like passions/nature with you"), not simply "fellow human." The term ὁμοιοπαθής is significant—it's the same word used in Acts 14:15 (Paul and Barnabas at Lystra) and James 5:17. The Cornelius episode in Acts 10:26 has Peter say "ἀνάστηθι· καὶ ἐγὼ αὐτὸς ἄνθρωπός εἰμι." Epiphanius's wording differs, using ὁμοιοπαθής. The brief should note this precise wording or acknowledge the adaptation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Epiphanius writes to oppose the practice of making painted images of Christ, Mary, martyrs, angels, and prophets for memorial and honor, which he regards as a return to idolatry
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Λόγος τοῦ ἁγίου ̓Επιφανίου κατὰ τῶν ἐπιτηδευόντων ποιεῖν εἰδωλικῷ θεσμῷ εἰκόνας εἰς ἀφομοίωσιν τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ τῆς Θεοτόκου καὶ τῶν μαρτύρων, ετι δὲ καὶ ἀγγέλων καὶ προφητῶν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The title specifies εἰδωλικῷ θεσμῷ ("by an idolatrous custom/law"), which the brief renders as "for memorial and honor." The opponents' stated motive (μνημόσυνον καὶ τιμήν) appears in v.2, but the occasion description conflates the author's characterization with the opponents' defense. Better: "Epiphanius writes to oppose the practice of making images of Christ, the Theotokos, martyrs, angels, and prophets according to an idolatrous custom; his opponents claim they do this for memorial and honor."

_unresolved_facts.claim: Moses, who: "Cited as unable to gaze upon the incomprehensible God, showing that God cannot be depicted"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: 12 πῶς τὸν ἀκατάληπτον καὶ ἀνεκδιήγητον καὶ ἀπερινόητον ἀπερίγραφόν τε γράφειν λέγει τις, ον οὐκ ι σχυσε Μωυσῆς ἀτενίσαι;
_unresolved_facts.fix: Moses is cited as unable to gaze upon (ἀτενίσαι) the one who is incomprehensible, indescribable, inconceivable, and uncircumscribable. The brief says "unable to gaze upon the incomprehensible God," but the text does not say "God" explicitly here—it uses relative pronoun ὃν referring back to the one described with these negative attributes. The Christological context (v.13-14 discusses Christ's incarnation) suggests this may refer to the incarnate Christ or the divine nature, not simply "God" in general. Better: "Cited as unable to gaze upon the incomprehensible and uncircumscribable one (Christ/God), showing that he cannot be depicted."
